blocks.caption: Real output (z3-solver 5.4.1). The counterexample strings are whatever the solver finds first; any principal other than students and tas works.

blocks.title: From a policy to a proof or a counterexample

scenes.caption: Policy X lets students read Exam.pdf and TAs read Exam.pdf and Answer.pdf. Policy Y allows anyone getObject on cs240/* and denies students Answer.pdf.
Is X at most as permissive as Y? The solver looks for a request X allows and Y denies, finds none, and so proves it for every possible request.
Does Y allow only students and TAs? The solver returns a request from some other principal: Y makes the bucket publicly readable, exactly the paper's point.
Simplified: the real engine also encodes conditions (source IP, VPC, prefixes), case-insensitive matching and many policy types, and asks a sequence of refining questions.

blocks.md:
You meet Zelkova through **IAM Access Analyzer** (IAM: AWS Identity and Access Management, the service that holds these policies). Its documentation says it "uses a technology called Zelkova" that "translates IAM policies into equivalent logical statements" and "applies Zelkova repeatedly to a policy, using increasingly specific queries" to describe what external access a policy grants ([AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access-analyzer-concepts.html)). The same docs note it does not examine access logs: a finding says what is possible, not what happened.

**s2n-tls** is AWS's open-source TLS library. Galois, a formal methods company, proved its HMAC and DRBG (deterministic random bit generator) implementations equivalent to specifications in Cryptol, Galois's specification language, using its Software Analysis Workbench (SAW), and wired the proofs into continuous integration so they re-run on every code change ([Galois](https://galois.com/project/amazon-s2n/)).

**Cedar** is an open-source authorisation policy language from AWS (policies are permit and forbid rules over principals, actions and resources). Its design paper says the language was "finely balanced to allow for a sound and complete logical encoding", so policy changes can be checked to not alter permissions, and that Cedar is "modeled ... in the Lean programming language" with key properties proved in Lean's proof assistant ([arXiv 2403.04651](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.04651)).

The companion paper names the process **verification-guided development**: prove properties of an executable model, then use differential random testing (run model and production Rust on the same random inputs and compare) to check the code matches. Proofs found "4 bugs in Cedar's policy validator"; differential and property-based testing found "21 additional bugs" ([arXiv 2407.01688](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01688)).

Defender use: run Access Analyzer (or an equivalent policy checker) in CI so a pull request that makes a resource externally accessible fails before deployment, and alert on new external-access findings in production. Treat a finding as "this access is possible"; confirm actual use from CloudTrail logs (AWS's record of API calls).

blocks.question: A Zelkova-style check of "policy Y allows only students and TAs" returns unsat. What does that mean?
options: The solver ran out of time
Some request from another principal is allowed
The policy is syntactically invalid
No request from anyone else is allowed by Y, for every possible principal, action and resource
blocks.explain: The question is encoded as: find a request Y allows whose principal is neither students nor tas. Unsat means no such request exists, so the property holds for all requests, not only the ones someone thought to test.

blocks.question: How did Cedar's team check that the production Rust matches the Lean model they proved properties about?
options: They proved the Rust code correct line by line in Lean
Differential random testing: run the model and the Rust on the same random inputs and compare results
Code review only
They compiled Lean to Rust
blocks.explain: Proofs cover the model; differential random testing connects the model to the production code, and property-based testing covers unmodelled parts. Together these found 21 bugs beyond the 4 found by proofs.

lessons.title: Model checking a distributed security protocol with TLA+

blocks.md:
Not every security protocol involves cryptography. Revoking a stolen session token across several servers is a distributed protocol with a security invariant: once the administrator is told "revoked", no server accepts the token again. The Formal verification of systems code course taught TLA+ (Temporal Logic of Actions) and TLC (its explicit-state model checker) on consensus; here the same tools check a security property.

The design: an admin service sends the revocation to every replica, each replica keeps its own copy of the revocation list, and the admin sees "revoked" when the service confirms. The attacker holds the stolen token and keeps presenting it to any replica it likes.

blocks.code:
---------------------------- MODULE Revoke ----------------------------
\* An admin revokes a stolen token; replicas check their own copy of
\* the revocation list. Safety: after "revoked", no replica accepts it.
EXTENDS Naturals
CONSTANTS Replicas, WaitForAcks, Durable

VARIABLES sent, known, acks, done, badAccept
vars == <<sent, known, acks, done, badAccept>>

Init == /\ sent = FALSE            \* revoke message sent?
        /\ known = [r \in Replicas |-> FALSE]
        /\ acks = {}
        /\ done = FALSE            \* admin sees "revoked"
        /\ badAccept = FALSE

SendRevoke == /\ ~sent /\ sent' = TRUE
              /\ UNCHANGED <<known, acks, done, badAccept>>

Deliver(r) == /\ sent /\ ~known[r]
              /\ known' = [known EXCEPT ![r] = TRUE]
              /\ acks' = acks \cup {r}
              /\ UNCHANGED <<sent, done, badAccept>>

Confirm == /\ sent /\ ~done
           /\ (WaitForAcks => acks = Replicas)
           /\ done' = TRUE
           /\ UNCHANGED <<sent, known, acks, badAccept>>

Accept(r) == /\ ~known[r]           \* replica still thinks token is valid
             /\ badAccept' = (badAccept \/ done)
             /\ UNCHANGED <<sent, known, acks, done>>

Restart(r) == /\ known' = [known EXCEPT ![r] = Durable /\ known[r]]
              /\ UNCHANGED <<sent, acks, done, badAccept>>

Next == \/ SendRevoke \/ Confirm
        \/ \E r \in Replicas : Deliver(r) \/ Accept(r) \/ Restart(r)

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars
NoAcceptAfterRevoke == ~badAccept
=========================================================================
blocks.caption: Written for this course. WaitForAcks and Durable are design choices, set as constants in the model configuration. Restart models a replica process restarting and reloading its list.

blocks.md: Read the actions as the attacker and the environment see them. `Accept(r)` can happen at any time: the attacker presents the token, and if replica r has not heard of the revocation it accepts, which is a violation if the admin was already told "revoked". `Restart(r)` models a crash and restart: with `Durable = FALSE` the replica's in-memory list is lost. `Confirm` is the moment the admin sees success. TLC explores every interleaving of these steps for two replicas.

blocks.code:
$ java -cp tla2tools.jar tlc2.TLC -config buggy.cfg Revoke.tla   # WaitForAcks=FALSE
Error: Invariant NoAcceptAfterRevoke is violated.
State 2: <SendRevoke ...>   State 3: <Confirm ...>   State 4: <Accept ...>
7 distinct states found

# WaitForAcks=TRUE, Durable=FALSE
Error: Invariant NoAcceptAfterRevoke is violated.
State 2: <SendRevoke>  3: <Deliver>  4: <Restart>  5: <Deliver>
State 6: <Confirm>  7: <Accept>
14 distinct states found

# WaitForAcks=TRUE, Durable=TRUE
Model checking completed. No error has been found.
6 distinct states found
blocks.caption: Real TLC 2.19 results (tla2tools.jar v1.7.4 from the tlaplus releases page, run with Java from a scratch folder), condensed to the action names of each counterexample. Each config also sets Replicas = {r1, r2} and CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE.

blocks.title: TLC's second counterexample: an acknowledged revocation forgotten

scenes.caption: The admin service sends the revocation to both replicas. WaitForAcks is on: it will only confirm after every replica has acknowledged.
r1 stores the revocation in memory and acknowledges. Its ack is now counted.
r1 restarts. Durable is off, so its in-memory list is gone, but the ack it already sent stays counted.
r2 receives the revocation and acknowledges. All acks are in, so the service confirms and the admin is told "revoked".
The attacker presents T to r1, which no longer knows about the revocation and accepts it. The invariant is broken after a confirmed revocation.

blocks.md:
The first bug is the obvious one: confirming before replicas know. The second is the kind TLC is good at: acknowledgement plus volatile state. Each step is reasonable in isolation, and the bad order needs a restart in a narrow window, which tests rarely produce. The fix the model checker accepts is to make the revocation **durable before acknowledging** (write it to disk or a replicated log, then ack), so a restart cannot undo it.

The same exploration in Python, as a check that nothing magic happens inside TLC:

blocks.caption: A breadth-first explorer mirroring Revoke.tla: same actions, same invariant. Plain python3.

blocks.code:
$ python3 revoke.py
WaitForAcks=False Durable=False VIOLATED: SendRevoke -> Confirm -> Accept(r1)
WaitForAcks=True  Durable=False VIOLATED: SendRevoke -> Deliver(r1) -> Restart(r1) -> Deliver(r2) -> Confirm -> Accept(r1)
WaitForAcks=True  Durable=True  holds in all 6 reachable states
blocks.caption: Real output: the same two counterexamples as TLC, and the same 6 reachable states for the fixed design.

blocks.md: The model is small on purpose: two replicas, one token, no message loss or duplication. A real design review would add those environment actions (the Formal verification of systems code course shows how) and a liveness property (the revocation eventually completes). A passing check is only as strong as the environment you allowed.

blocks.question: TLC finds no violation with WaitForAcks = TRUE and Durable = TRUE. Which change to the model would most likely bring a new counterexample worth investigating?
options: Add an action that lets a replica restore its list from an old backup
Rename the replicas
Remove the Accept action
Reduce to one replica
blocks.explain: Restoring an old snapshot re-creates the volatile-state problem through a different door. Removing Accept or replicas makes the model weaker and hides bugs; renaming changes nothing.

blocks.question: Why is the second counterexample hard to find by testing the real system?
options: It needs a quantum attacker
It only happens with more than 100 replicas
It needs a restart in a narrow window between acknowledging and confirming, an interleaving tests rarely produce
TLC invents behaviours the real system cannot have
blocks.explain: The failure needs a specific order of independent events. Exhaustive exploration tries every order of the modelled steps; tests sample a few.

lessons.title: Where proofs stop: models, side channels and wrong specs

blocks.md: Every lesson so far has shown a boundary. This one collects them, because the most common way verified systems fail is at a boundary nobody wrote down. CyBOK names the two central limits: "one verifies properties of models, not the actual systems used", and "one may simply fail to specify all relevant system requirements". To which you can add: the tools and their assumptions are trusted, and side channels are usually outside the model.

**Real case: KRACK (2017).** Wi-Fi's WPA2 four-way handshake had security proofs. Mathy Vanhoef and Frank Piessens showed that by manipulating and replaying handshake messages, so that message 3 arrives again, an attacker makes a client **reinstall** a key it is already using, which resets the packet number (the nonce) and replay counter of the encryption layer; nonce reuse then lets traffic be decrypted or forged depending on the cipher. Their paper is precise about why the proofs did not help: "our attacks do not violate the security properties proven in formal analysis", because "the proofs do not model key installation" ([CCS 2017](https://papers.mathyvanhoef.com/ccs2017.pdf)). Matthew Green, a cryptographer at Johns Hopkins University, put it this way: the handshake and the encryption protocol were each studied in isolation, and "apparently nobody looked closely at the two components as they were connected together" ([blog](https://blog.cryptographyengineering.com/2017/10/16/falling-through-the-kracks/)).

scenes.caption: The chain from intent to running system. Only the model to proof step is machine-checked in a typical protocol analysis.
Requirement gap: the goal was never stated. QUIC's analyses lacked a client-authentication goal; TLS 1.3 clients cannot tell if the server accepted their certificate.
Model gap: the model omits behaviour that matters. KRACK: the handshake proofs did not model when keys are installed.
Unverified parts: CompCert's front-end bugs, the C glue around verified primitives, an implementation mistake like goto fail.
Physical gap: timing and cache channels below the model. Dragonblood's password leaks; seL4's confidentiality proof excludes timing.

Lining up the course's cases against that chain:

- **Missing or wrong goal**: the QUIC 0-RTT unknown key share went unnoticed because no analysis "formulate[d] an authentication goal that exposed the flaw"; the TLS 1.3 client-certificate gap is a goal the standard chose not to provide.
- **Missing assumption**: 5G-AKA's dependence on unstated channel properties, which let an operator conform and still be insecure.
- **Model omits behaviour**: KRACK's key reinstallation.
- **Unverified component**: CompCert's front-end; goto fail (from TLS and PKI in practice), a duplicated line that skipped signature checking in code no protocol proof touches.
- **Below the model**: Dragonblood's timing and cache leaks; seL4's excluded timing channels.

Vanhoef and Piessens add a social warning: "formal proofs may in fact be counterproductive: once a protocol is formally verified, the community may become less interested in auditing actual implementations". The response is not to distrust proofs but to read them like contracts. For any "formally verified" claim, ask:

1. **Which artefact?** Design model, source code, or binary?
2. **Which properties?** Exact secrecy, agreement or equivalence statements, and under which attacker and compromise model.
3. **Which assumptions?** Primitives, channels, compiler, hardware, configuration.
4. **What is excluded?** Timing, unverified glue, liveness, denial of service.
5. **Does it still match?** Proofs re-run in CI on every change, as for s2n, or a one-off result on an old draft?

A proof moves risk from "did we test enough" to "did we state the right thing, and do the assumptions hold". Put your review effort where the proof stops: the goals, the model's omissions, the trusted components and the side channels.

**Where to practise.** Everything here runs on a laptop with no special hardware:

- The [Tamarin manual](https://tamarin-prover.com/manual/) walks through writing and proving protocol models; the repository's `examples/classic` folder holds NSPK3 and NSLPK3 from lesson 6.
- The [ProVerif manual](https://bblanche.gitlabpages.inria.fr/proverif/manual.pdf) has a tutorial chapter and many example models.
- [Learn TLA+](https://learntla.com/) teaches specification and model checking for designs like lesson 14.
- The [Z3 guide](https://microsoft.github.io/z3guide/) teaches SMT queries in the browser, a good next step from lessons 10 and 13.

A good first exercise: model a protocol you use at work, state its goals as lemmas, and add an exists-trace sanity lemma before trusting any result.

blocks.question: The WPA2 four-way handshake had security proofs, yet KRACK broke WPA2 in practice. According to the KRACK paper, why?
options: The proofs contained a mathematical error
KRACK broke AES
The proofs assumed a passive attacker
The proven properties (key secrecy, authentication) still held; the models did not include when keys are installed, so reinstallation and nonce reset were outside them
blocks.explain: KRACK does not leak the session key and does not violate the proven properties. The gap was in the model: key installation was not part of it, and reinstalling a key resets nonces used by the encryption layer.

blocks.question: A vendor says their protocol library is "formally verified". Which question best exposes the most likely gap?
options: Which artefact was verified (model, source or binary), against which stated properties, and under what assumptions and exclusions?
Which proof assistant did you use?
How many lines of proof are there?
Was the proof peer reviewed?
blocks.explain: Tool choice and proof size say little. The useful answer pins down the artefact, the exact properties, and what is assumed or excluded, which is where the KRACK, CompCert and Dragonblood cases all sit.

blocks.question: Which pairing of case and gap is correct?
options: Dragonblood: missing authentication goal
KRACK: unverified compiler front-end
QUIC 0-RTT UKS: no client-authentication goal in earlier analyses
seL4: timing channels are covered by the confidentiality proof
blocks.explain: The Inria paper says earlier QUIC analyses did not formulate the authentication goal that exposed the flaw. Dragonblood is a side channel, KRACK a model omission, and seL4 explicitly excludes timing channels.
